stimulus: A meteorologist launches a weather balloon carrying a temperature sensor. At the moment of launch, the sensor reads $22^\circ\text{C}$. As the balloon rises, the temperature it records drops by $3^\circ\text{C}$ for every $500$ meters of altitude it gains. The function $T$ gives the temperature, in degrees Celsius, recorded by the sensor when the balloon is $h$ kilometers above the launch site.
explanation: Start with the value when the input is 0. At $h = 0$ the sensor reads $22$, so that is the constant term. Next, find the rate per single unit of the input. The input is in kilometers, but the drop is given per $500$ meters. One kilometer is two lots of $500$ meters, so the temperature drops $2 \times 3 = 6$ degrees per kilometer. The temperature is falling, so the rate is negative: $T(h) = 22 - 6h$. Then $T(3) = 22 - 18 = 4$.

common_errors.why: Used 3 degrees per kilometer without converting from 'per 500 meters', so got 22 - 3(3) = 13.
Converted the wrong way and halved the rate to 1.5 degrees per kilometer instead of doubling it: 22 - 1.5(3) = 17.5.
Gave the slope the wrong sign and added the drop even though the temperature is falling: 22 + 6(3) = 40.
Made both errors: no unit conversion and a positive slope, so 22 + 3(3) = 31.

stem: For $n \ge 4$, the total fee $C$, in dollars, for the laboratory to analyze $n$ samples can be written as $C = 12n + k$, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
stimulus: A nutrition science laboratory measures the vitamin content of food samples for outside researchers. The laboratory charges a flat fee of $\$90$, which covers the analysis of up to $4$ samples. Each sample beyond the first $4$ costs an additional $\$12$.
explanation: The $\$12$ charge applies only to samples after the first $4$, so the number of extra samples is $n - 4$. That gives $C = 90 + 12(n - 4)$. Distribute: $C = 90 + 12n - 48 = 12n + 42$. So $k = 42$. Check with $n = 4$: $12(4) + 42 = 90$, which is the flat fee, as it should be.

common_errors.why: Ignored the threshold and charged $12 for every sample, including the 4 already covered: C = 90 + 12n.
Wrote 90 + 12(n - 4) but distributed the -4 with the wrong sign, adding 48 instead of subtracting it.
Treated only the first sample as covered and used (n - 1), so got 90 - 12 = 78.
Stopped at the 12 × 4 = 48 adjustment and reported it as the constant.

stimulus: A paleobotanist studies fossil pollen in a sediment core taken from a lake bed. The sediment at the top of the core, at a depth of $0$ centimeters, was deposited $1{,}200$ years ago. Going deeper into the core, every $5$ centimeters of depth represents another $200$ years. The age $A$, in years, of the sediment at a depth of $d$ centimeters is modeled by $A(d) = md + c$, where $m$ and $c$ are constants.
explanation: The input is depth in centimeters and the output is age in years, so $m$ is years per centimeter. You are told the age rises $200$ years for every $5$ centimeters. Divide to get the rate for one centimeter: $200 \div 5 = 40$ years per centimeter. The constant is the age at depth $0$, so $c = 1200$, and the model is $A(d) = 40d + 1200$. The question asks for $m$, which is $40$.

common_errors.why: Inverted the rate and computed centimeters per year (5 ÷ 200) instead of years per centimeter.
Used the 'per 5 centimeters' figure as if it were per centimeter and did not divide by 5.
Swapped the starting value and the rate, giving the age at the top of the core as the slope.

stimulus: A printmaker is producing an edition of two-color relief prints and starts with $400$ milliliters of ink. Before printing, $25$ milliliters are used to roll out the inking slab. Each print is made from two separate blocks, one for each color, and each block uses $9$ milliliters of ink for every $3$ prints. The amount of ink $I$, in milliliters, left after $p$ prints is modeled by $I(p) = a - bp$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants.
explanation: $b$ is the amount of ink used per print. For one block, $9$ milliliters covers $3$ prints, which is $9 \div 3 = 3$ milliliters per print. Every print uses two blocks, so the total is $2 \times 3 = 6$ milliliters per print. The setup ink only changes the starting amount: $a = 400 - 25 = 375$. So $I(p) = 375 - 6p$, and $b = 6$.

common_errors.why: Found the per-print rate for one block but ignored that each print uses two blocks.
Doubled for the two blocks but did not divide the 'per 3 prints' figure: 2 × 9 = 18.
Multiplied 9 by 3 instead of dividing and also ignored the second block.
Multiplied 9 by 3 instead of dividing, then doubled for the two blocks.
Swapped the starting value and the rate, giving a (the ink left after setup) instead of b.
